Chartered banks are private institutions and they should never take the place of the state. Nevertheless, this is exactly what happens when chartered banks create new credit out of thin air.
I realize that it is interesting for a bank such as the Bank of Western Canada, with an authorized capital of $25 million to be able to multiply it 12J times and lend to Canadian citizens, school boards, municipalities, provinces and even the federal government up to 12-J times the value of its liquid assets, a value which it does not have but on which, being a favoured bank, it would earn interest.
We submit that if we have to keep for another few years this nonsensical system, this function should at least be entrusted to provincial chartered banks; thus, the provincial governments, more enlightened than the federal government, would allow their people to share in the benefits.
But no, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) even refuses to the provinces the old right they had to acquire 10 per cent of bank shares. The Minister of Finance must be interested indeed in the bank trust to place such severe restrictions on the provinces.
It would be interesting to know how many members of both old-line parties-and they seem to be united on this matter-will support this motion of the Minister of Finance.
Certainly the day has not yet come when members of parliament will realize that only the Bank of Canada is responsible for creating new credit likely to get the economy moving, as it is its responsibility to keep the accounts of the country, so that Canadian citizens may benefit from Canada's financial surpluses.
If it were not legalized by an act of parliament, I would say we are witnessing, without being able to do anything about it, the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on the people by a small group of financiers who contribute to the election of members of this house. In my opinion, this is the most abominable act of treachery a member could commit against the people.
I realize that, in the case of many members, they just do not know any better, and that is why I urge them to make a thorough study

of our present banking system, so they can appreciate the pressing need for reform, mainly as regards chartered banks and especially the provision of new credit.
Many imagine that we are the sworn enemies of chartered banks. Nothing is farther from the truth. We feel that chartered banks have a very important part to play in our financial system and we want them to perform their functions to the full, but not to take on those of the Bank of Canada.
Once again, we maintain that the Bank of Canada ought to act in the public field while the chartered banks should limit their activities to the private field.
It is up to the Bank of Canada to control and to issue, not only the legal currency, but also monetary credit. Therefore, we are the greatest protectors of the chartered banks, since we want them to do their own work only and we will not tolerate their intervention in other fields, even if it were for their own good financially.
We agree that chartered banks may lend their depositors and shareholders' money, that they may operate up to 100 per cent of their liquid assets.
I am not asking that chartered banks be subject to the same strict control as credit unions, which only lend 50 per cent of their assets, and this constitutes, besides, discrimination against credit unions which also form an integral part of our financial system.
Why has a small group of millionaires obtained so many favours from the governments at the expense of the working classes who are the shareholders in the credit unions? In my opinion, this is the rankest injustice ever contrived by a monetary system which subdues the people more and more instead of providing them with sensible means of distribution.
This formula was devised by the great minds of international finance in their eagerness to control the people.
Certain rather surprising actions, to say the least, of former and even present ministers show their close connections with financial groups. In view of their concern for financial interests, one wonders whether they were elected to represent the people or the financial interests.
Is it normal for a member of parliament to be a director or even the president of a chartered bank or to have interests in most finance companies? Yet, Mr. Speaker, there is ample proof that such is the case.
Do you think the public is unaware of this little set-up? Thirty or 40 years ago, you
May 13, 1965



could fool the public but people no longer believe in Santa Claus. The web of fairy tales and aura of mystery which was wound around the monetary system until recently, is gradually falling apart, and very soon the parties involved will have to tell the public the truth.
The Canadian people will have to be told that their country is productive and that that production and the wealth it creates should benefit the whole population-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the debate was adjourned at five o'clock we were considering resolution No. 5, more precisely paragraph (b) which deals mainly with mak-22620-82
National Housing Act
ing loans and grants relating to urban renewal.
I gave as an example of urban renewal a pilot project carried out in Montreal, namely the "Habitations Jeanne-Mance", under which 796 dwellings were built between Sanguinet street, St. Lawrence boulevard, Ontario and Demontigny streets, which could house 2,697 people at the end of 1963, according to a statement made on March 2, 1964 by the minister responsible for Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation.
The minister also stated at that time that the cost of acquiring land and buildings amounted to $6,883,406, the cost of tearing down slums to $185,918 and the construction costs to $10,667,912, for a total of $17,083,133 to be amortized over a 50-year period.
Besides, it should be noted that those housing units will have to be maintained and there will be 14 people working for the "Habitations Jeanne-Mance", a limited dividend corporation in charge of the project.
In 1963-again according to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-the maintenance costs of those housing units amounted to $128,733. It is expected that the cost will go up in the future, because of salary raises to be granted, no doubt, to the maintenance staff and because of the downgrading or depreciation of the housing units.
To pay for those costs, the Habitations Jeanne-Mance Corporation took in $536,805 in rent during 1963.
The result is that to amortize the capital invested and pay the interests and maintenance costs there was an operating deficit of $421,764 for the year 1963.
If we figure the annual receipts and deficits, we can see that in 1963 the total repayment cost amounted to $958,569. If we multiply this figure by 50, which is the number of years required to repay the total amount, we arrive to the fantastic sum of $47,928,450 for 796 housing units, which represents more than $60,000 for each of those units at the end of 50 years.
During that period, the 796 tenants will have paid, according to the average $50 rent, an amount of $23,880,000, or a total yearly rent of $600 per tenant, or $30,000 during 50 years.
During the same period, supposing that the operation and maintenance costs, together with the compulsory reimbursement of capital and interest charges remain the same, the losses amounting to $421,764 in 1963, the total of those operating deficits will reach $21,088,200 after 50 years.

May 13. 1965
National Housing Act
If we add to that money invested by the federal government, the Quebec government and the city of Montreal for the demolition, clearing of land and purchase of land as well as the rebuilding, amounting to a total of $17,088,133, we find that to $38,161,133 has been spent by the governments. This amounts to a total and final cost of $60,000 per unit, at the end of 50 years being paid by the provincial and federal governments.
It can then be concluded that if the federal government and the city of Montreal, instead of building the "Habitations Jeanne-Mance", had simply advanced the necessary money, without interest, to the families involved, allowing them to build their own homes, it would have been possible to build five units with the same amount instead of only one as in the "Habitations Jeanne-Mance".
With $47 million invested in the Jeanne-Mance housing project, it would have been possible to build 4,000 units instead of 796.
Under the present C.M.H.C. system, which assisted various housing projects, including urban housing projects, it costs the tenants at the end of 60 years an average of $60,000, representing both capital and interest, including also the amounts spent by the federal and provincial governments and the city of Montreal.
In adopting the formula whereby interest-free loans would have been made to tenants in order to have their own homes built, the governments would have lost nothing in extending the repayment period on a $12,000 loan, for instance, over a 30-year period, meaning 360 monthly payments of $33.33, to which, however, taxes and fuel costs would have to be added, of course, bringing the total monthly payment to about $50, which is what tenants in the Jeanne-Mance project are now paying, with this difference however that in 30 years, those families would own their own homes after having paid $12,000 to repay their loan or $18,000 if taxes and fuel are included.
But today after having spent $30,000 in rent for 50 years, those families will still be tenants.
Under our present system, we find that, as in the case of the Habitations Jeanne-Mance, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation spent $60,000 per unit. It means that in his lifetime a tenant will pay the equivalent of five houses since it can be said that a house costs about $12,000 and, at the end of 50 years he will not even own a little bungalow.
There is no solution under our present system. What the Creditistes have always

advocated is this. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should use the banks or other similar institutions to make interest-free loans to those who want to build.
A Creditiste government would solve the housing and slum problem in the following manner: loans for construction of family dwellings to be occupied by the owner would be loans for the social development, for the development of this country's social capital and not for making profits available to individuals.
Social Credit claims that social investment capital should not come from the private sector, which forces borrowers to repay two, three, four and even five times the amount borrowed, but that it should be made up of new credit, that is of new bank credit.
This argument is supported by the director of the Brussels International Superior Institute of Town Planning, Mr. Gaston Bardet, who said:
How can we build the 200,000 houses needed every year? Ask the bankers how they proceed when building for themselves. What does a bank do when it wants to build? It is going over to another bank for a loan? Of course not. The bank opens a current credit account for itself on which, of course, it pays no interest. It buys the site and pays the contractors by cheques guaranteed.. .by the building itself. Then it draws rents and, at the end of 30 years, the money collected is in balance with the credit account opened. The operation is written off, but the bank keeps the building which it now owns without having paid a penny, except perhaps the cost of entering on the ledger the amounts written under assets and liabilities.
So, the bank, thanks to modern credit, using scrip money, in other words the solvency of credit was able to create fictitious money and to convert it into a real building, cheques issued being cancelled at the end of 30 years after the magic operation is over.
According to Social Credit, there is no magic in that. To create then destroy the credit which is, during its existence, just as good as real money, is what banks are actually doing under the authority conferred upon them.
The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or any other similar body should act as a bank for those who want to build their own homes, and provide future owners with the money they need.
The bank would grant the necessary loans to buy the lot and to build the house according to
recognized standards.
After a study of the family's ability to repay, the bank would decide the monthly repayment to be made.
The loans would be interest free and the monthly repayments would be made over a period of 20, 30 or even 40 years, depending on the quality of materials used and the repayment ability.
As a general policy, this monthly rent could be 20 per cent of the monthly income, as it is the case with the "Habitations Jeanne-Mance", for instance.
Thousands of tenant families could become home owners and a stabilizing force in our society, while
May 13, 1965

still being a source of income for the municipalities. Finally, the families would feel more at home and could enjoy a sound affluence and freedom which would allow them to better provide for the maintenance and education of their children.
Mr. Chairman, our construction policy, with the assistance of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, enables people to acquire their own home, but they have to pay five times the cost price.
In an intelligent financial system, the credits of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would be made available to borrowers without interest and the instalments to repay the loan would be kept in line with the depreciation of the property, namely the buildings. If a house is good to last 20 years, according to the figures and the standards of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, repayment could be made over a 20 year basis and then a property would have been paid only once and not five times in financing costs. Nowadays, many home owners must pay for a lifetime, as is the case with the "Habitations Jeanne-Mance". They must pay for their home and after 50 years, they will not even own a house. They are paying because our financial system is not consistent with progress and with the abundance of wealth in the country. They have to pay the equivalent of five properties and after 50 years, they do not even own a home. That is why we, the Creditistes, do not claim that we will give a house to everybody, but we want to set up a financial system to enable every family to buy a house and to pay for it without making every family pay for five houses in financing costs while remaining tenants.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN ADVANCES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should not like the occasion of the discussion of this legislation to pass without taking the opportunity to address a few words to the House on the question of urban renewal, and more particularly that aspect of it which provides for subsidized public housing for people of low incomes. This is of particular importance to me because I think there is probably no other constituency in the country with such a high concentration of urban renewal developments of this kind, and which also in the downtown part of it provides such a great challenge from the standpoint of urban renewal.
National Housing Act
Members of the House who have taken some cognizance of the Toronto newspapers in recent days cannot have escaped noticing the attention that has been paid to the difficulties that have arisen in the St. James Town area and more particularly the plight of the unfortunate people in that area who will be ousted from the very substandard housing which is being replaced by apartment developments. The problem of bad housing on St. James and Ontario Streets and on Darling and Rose Avenues has not been solved and will not be solved merely by levelling the existing buildings in the way that many have already been levelled and replacing them with shiny new apartments. The problem really has only been shifted to another locale somewhere else in the downtown area where the St. James Town residents because of limited means, will have to move to find shelter-and very inadequate shelter at that.
Here, Mr. Chairman, I would make it very clear that I am not expressing any criticism of Mr. Bradley or the Toronto Housing Corporation, who I know have been doing their very best to find shelter for these people. Rather, the difficulties of the present administration in Toronto have been created because their hands are tied, because there is not a sufficient stock of adequate housing in the city for people of limited incomes to which the St. James Town residents can be moved.
The root of the problem is an economic one in that the incomes of these families are simply not adequate to meet the expenses involved in living in the centre of the city, expenses which are contributed to a very great extent by the high level of rents in downtown accommodation. Inadequate housing is a cancer in the very heart of a large modem city, a cancer that will just not go away by wishing it would or by turning one's back on it. Like a cancer it spreads and will kill neighbouring areas in increasingly large numbers unless dramatic action is taken to stop it.
The St. James Town situation which has occurred in my riding is not an isolated one in my city. It is not of recent origin and it is not the responsibility of only one or two slum operators. In fact, these people are really only ghouls who are feeding on the dying neighbourhood, but they are not solely responsible for having killed the neighbourhood. Rather it has been the indifference and the shortsightedness of the community as a

May 13, 1965
National Housing Act
whole. It is all of us in that particular community who have been responsible for it, not only the elected representatives but those who have elected us and also, and just as directly those who live in areas remote from areas like St. James Town and who have failed to show the required interest in urban renewal.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
There is opposition, Mr. Speaker, to subsidized public housing, opposition such as that reflected in the remarks of the hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi this afternoon when he observed on behalf of his party that the Conservatives have always believed in the principles of ownership democracy. I point out that ownership democracy leaves little room for people like the people of St. James Town who have not the benefit of economic means of securing ownership in housing, and who are really hard put to provide adequate rental housing. I think that philosophy was obvious with regard to the former government for, as the hon. Member for Hamilton West pointed out this afternoon, that government contributed nothing to the provisions of the National Housing Act in respect of urban renewal, except to increase the lending limit by an amount equivalent to one-eighth of the amount the present Government is asking Parliament to approve in this particular resolution.
Much of that opposition, Mr. Chairman, whether it is opposition by hon. Members opposite or opposition by the community at large, is rooted in misunderstanding of the economics of urban renewal, or the extent to which the participation of senior levels of Government, the very substantial financial assistance senior levels of Government are prepared to make available for urban renewal, extend the municipal tax base and relieve the individual municipal taxpayer from increases in municipal taxes which otherwise would be inevitable. Perhaps I might refer in this connection to the following study made in the Toronto Star for November 22, 1962, which hon. Members will recognize is still very much apropos. I quote:
When you see new offices, apartment blocks and other buildings going up, it means the tax burden on your home is being held down.
One of Toronto's new apartment projects and a new office building illustrate this benefit from redeveloping older areas.
Together they are paying $351,334 in taxes this year. This is more than 15 times the $22,925 in taxes the same two pieces of land produced when private dwellings occupied them.

Hon. Members will recognize at once, and I think people generally recognize at once, the value to the community of new commercial assessment. It is well known. What appears not to be as well recognized is that public housing projects also pay their way in municipal assessment, just as new commercial projects do. Projects such as the Moss Park development, which has recently gone into occupancy in my constituency, contribute just as much to the municipal coffers as do commercial properties. What is more, they replace at the same time run-down, low value areas which in themselves create heavy social costs by way of welfare, fire and police protection.
I should like to refer for a moment, Mr. Chairman, to the potential financial benefits for the City of Toronto from extensive urban renewal, which will become clear when one bears in mind that under the amendments introduced by this Government last year, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is now prepared to lend up to 90 per cent of the cost of the public housing project and to contribute up to 50 per cent of the subsidies necessary to meet the operating deficits of these projects. In the case of Toronto only 7.5 per cent of the operating costs of new projects will now fall upon the city taxpayers. In addition to the 50 per cent contribution of the Federal Government, the Ontario Housing Corporation is now prepared to contribute 42.5 per cent of this subsidy. Through this joint action of the two senior levels of government the municipality, therefore, is being given the opportunity for substantial redevelopment of the older areas at a fraction of the total capital cost.
May I just point out here, and I do not hesitate to do so, that I could not disagree more with the argument of the hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi this afternoon, when in the accents of Cassandra he decried what he described as a lack of federal-provincial co-operation in this field. As the Minister pointed out on the first day on which this subject was debated, the co-operation has been excellent. It has been nowhere more evident than it has been in the Province of Ontario where the Ontario Housing Corporation, under the leadership of Mr. Ken Soble .-and I will give the Provincial Government credit-has substantially followed in that direction, in concert with the initiative which this Government has given under the National Housing Act.
I should like to make reference particularly, Mr. Chairman, to the other areas of
May 13, 1965

my own constituency which have been considered in the City of Toronto Planning Board report entitled, "Improvement Program for Residential Areas", dated February, 1965. In that report it sets out that the most immediate areas for redevelopment are in the neighbourhood of Trefann Street, Sackville Place and Dermott Place, which are in the constituency of Rosedale, and Napier Place, which is in the constituency of Broadview. I think, further, I should cite the cost figures estimated for this development which will give hon. Members some idea just how much the Federal contribution is to these projects. It has been estimated by the City of Toronto Planning Board that the total cost would be $13,265,250. Of this amount, $9,793,125 would be contributed by the Federal Government and $2,340,163 by the Provincial Government. The balance, being somewhat in the neighbourhood of $2 million would be contributed by the two municipal levels of government, Metro Toronto and the City of Toronto. I think it is evident from that example that there is a terrific opportunity for the municipalities of this country, particularly my own city, to attempt to set right 50 to 70 years of neglect in order that the downtown area, many of the downtown areas such as the part I represent, may be made areas of Canada of which we can be proud, areas of Canada in which a family of limited means can enjoy good shelter.
I would close, Mr. Chairman, after these words of commendation of the Minister, with several remarks of exhortation to him, particularly with regard to a matter which I brought to his attention last year when the amendments to the National Housing Act were before Parliament. I referred at that time to the importance of recreational facilities in any large scale public housing development. As I mentioned, I have a very substantial amount of existing public housing development in my constituency, Regent Park, north and south, being perhaps the best known of the two. Unfortunately, these projects were developed with inadequate recreational facilities for the many thousands of children who are to be found there.
I should like to exhort the Minister not only to follow up his initiative and provide authority under the present legislation for new developments, but also extend the provisions of the National Housing Act so that the Federal Government may make loans to share in the development of recreational facilities to be established in existing devel-
National Housing Act
opments. This is good legislation, Mr. Chairman. This is legislation which will provide the funds with which to carry out the amendments we put through last year. I hope it will receive support from all parts of the House.

In the remarks I have to make on this resolution this evening, I do not intend to get lost in the streets of the City of Toronto. Every time I go there, I get lost. [DOT] (8:30 p.m.)

speechtext:
When I visit Toronto, Mr. Chairman, I do not go to Scarborough. Per-

May 13. 1965
National Housing Act
haps the hon. Member would not want me there anyway.
The hon. Member for Qu'Appelle stated that certain amendments had been made to the National Housing Act during the last few years. He said that during the ten years it has been in existence it has been amended eight times, twice by a Liberal Government and twice by a Conservative Government, and in this connection perhaps I may quote briefly from the hon. Member's speech:
This Act has been used by both parties in the Federal Government to take a part in the economy of Canada which I do not think could be matched by provinces working entirely by themselves. This Act is one of the classic examples of why the initiative in the economic Held should never be lost by the Federal Government, because no act, as I said earlier, has achieved as much as this one.
He was speaking of both parties in this regard. We who come from the Atlantic provinces have stressed in this House and in other places the need for a strong central government, and this is one of the best examples of that need.
I was pleased that the Minister gave us a complete statement of his activities as Minister responsible for this important Corporation. He told us he started his provincial meetings with Nova Scotia down where the East begins, and that he had a very successful meeting with the Premier and Cabinet of Nova Scotia. I am glad this was the case.
I know that in cities such as Halifax various urban renewal projects have been undertaken. I recall visiting there when the former Conservative Government was in power and seeing a low rental project being constructed, known as Mulgrave Park, which cost about $4 million. I went through it with the contractor, who happened to come from my own area, and I am glad to note the Minister is working with officials in that area in an effort to encourage further projects.
During the past year officials from the Minister's office in Halifax have visited Pictou County, my own constituency, and spoken to municipal officials in New Glasgow and Trenton. I do not know if an application has been made for an urban renewal study or survey, but if it has not been made I hope it soon will be. I understand the municipalities in that area are setting up such a survey, which I hope will receive the O.K. from the Federal Government. Several new industries are being developed there and there is a great need for new houses.
Some new houses are being constructed through the normal channels provided by the National Housing Act, and some are being
(Mr. MacEwan.]
built under commercial mortgages. However, I hope this survey is carried out because it is important that it be done before any really large projects are undertaken.
I listened with great interest this afternoon to the hon. Member for Spadina, as he comes from an area in which this legislation is most important. I was glad to note he mentioned a loan had been given to a university in his constituency to assist in the extension of it. All hon. Members will readily recall that this is a policy which was commenced by the former government. In Nova Scotia and the other Atlantic provinces university facilities have been greatly taxed. The universities have taken advantage of a certain provision in the Act, and I am glad this work is being carried on by the Minister and this Government because it means a lot to universities at the present time. We all know universities have other problems, but this policy of assistance has been of great help to them and I hope the Minister will continue it.
The hon. Member for Rosedale mentioned that there had been great co-operation between the Province of Ontario and the Federal Government. In Nova Scotia, the Nova Scotia Housing Commission, which was set up some time ago, and through which co-operative houses are constructed, makes applications to the Federal Government from time to time under the provisions of the National Housing Act.
In my own area a number of people have successfully undertaken these co-operative projects. Persons constructing such homes provide much of the labour themselves, thus cutting down the costs. Under both governments the federal department has cooperated greatly with these people, and I am sure will continue to do so. I know of several housing projects which are presently being submitted for approval and I hope they will receive sanction from the Federal Government at the earliest opportunity.
This afternoon the hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi mentioned that amendments were being proposed to the Bank Act. I do not intend to go into that subject because I know it would be out of order, but I wish to say it may assist housing in Canada. For example, I know of areas in my constituency, such as the mining town of Westville, where commercial mortgage loans are not made, and practically no loans under the National Housing Act.
I recall the very able spokesman for the Liberal Party, when in opposition, on national housing, the late hon. Member for
May 13, 1965

Nipissing, did an excellent job. I remember his putting forward the various viewpoints of his party, and asking the then Minister of Public Works to examine various changes that should be made in the act. Among the changes he advocated was the provision of mortgages for existing homes. This was also mentioned by the hon. Member for Spadina today, and I do not intend to deal with it fully except to suggest to the Minister that in future he should give consideration to doing something in that regard.
A constitutional argument was advanced by the hon. Member for Spadina who said the provinces and municipalities should O.K. the issuing of mortgages on existing houses. With the spirit of co-operative federalism that is about today, there should not be too much trouble in that proposal.
Another suggestion made by the Liberal opposition of that time was that the interest rates on N.H.A. mortgages should be reduced. Perhaps the Minister might look into that and some time in the future introduce amendments which would give effect to it.
The amendments outlined in the resolution are important. Regardless of what party is in power, this legislation is good. The Minister is proposing necessary amendments; and looking at the whole subject from an objective point of view I agree with the hon. Member for Hamilton West, who said this legislation must be flexible. In our changing country of today, and with the great expansion in urban areas, and some also in rural areas, flexibility must be continued in order to provide the housing which our people need. I hope the Minister will bear this in mind and that the legislation will be amended from time to time so as to provide the housing which Canadians deserve, and which is justly owed to them.

I rise to express briefly my support for this resolution. It is another step forward to meet a great and growing need in Canada. In the years that lie ahead the corporation will have a great opportunity to overcome the situation that we face today.
I have always appreciated the attitude taken by a former Minister, the late hon. Member from Nipissing, toward these matters, and all he did while he had the opportunity to promote the development of housing in this country. I am pleased the present Minister is continuing to speak in this House for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It always gives me great pleasure to see a thorough-going supporter of free enterprise responsible for a corporation which has a

He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words at this stage about the more important of the amendments to the Bank of Canada Act which are being proposed in this bill. It is, of course the intention that the bill be sent to the Banking and Commerce Committee as soon as it has received second reading so that hon. Members may have an opportunity to go into its various provisions in detail.
I should like to refer first of all to the proposed new section of the Act defining the relationship between the Government and the Bank of Canada in regard to monetary policy. It makes clear that there must be, as there is now, continuous consultation on monetary policy between the Government and the bank. It also provides a formal procedure whereby in the event of a disagreement between the Government and the bank which cannot be resolved, the Government may issue a directive to the bank as to the monetary policy that it is to follow.
It is proposed that any such directive should be in writing, should be in specific terms and applicable for a specified period, should be published forthwith in the Canada Gazette, and should be tabled in Parliament within 15 days. It is also proposed to eliminate the power which the Governor now has, but which has never been used, to veto any action or decision of the Board of Directors or of the Executive Committee of the bank.
The general objective of the proposed new section, which follows the recommendation of the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance, is to remove any doubt which may ever have existed about the responsibilities of the Government and the bank for monetary policy. As this bill is drafted, the Government can never shirk its ultimate responsibility for the monetary policy which is followed any more than it can for any field of national policy. The new section makes explicit this ultimate responsibility of the Government and specifies a statutory form of procedure under which it may be discharged.
If the Government exercises its right to insist on a change in monetary policy, it will be required to do so in a way which brings the issues to the attention of Parliament and the public. On the other hand, the directive power which is proposed in no way relieves the bank and the Governor of their responsibility for monetary policy and its execution. If the Government of the day ever issued a directive to the Governor to execute a mone-
May 13, 1965

tary policy which he felt was contrary to the public interest it can be presumed he would resign rather than accept such a responsibility.
Hon. Members may recall that the present Governor of the bank at the time of his appointment issued a statement setting forth views similar to those I have expressed today concerning the responsibilities of the bank and of the Government with regard to monetary policy. The existing relationship between bank and Government is based on these general principles and has worked very well in practice. The intent of the proposed amendment is not to change the basis of the existing relationship but rather to give it clear legislative recognition.
If I may add a personal word, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say how very fortunate we are to have Mr. Louis Rasminsky as Governor of the Bank of Canada.

1 come now to the proposal to empower the Bank of Canada to impose and vary a minimum secondary reserve requirement applicable to the chartered banks in replacement of its existing power to vary the minimum cash reserve requirement. Hon. Members will already be aware of the related changes which are being proposed in the bill to amend the Bank Act. Briefly, there are three proposed amendments, two to the Bank Act and one to the Bank of Canada Act, which would affect the reserve requirements of the chartered banks. The minimum average cash reserve requirement applicable to the chartered banks would be lowered gradually from 8 per cent of their Canadian dollar deposit liabilities to 7 per cent; the period over which daily cash reserves are averaged for the purpose of meeting the requirement would be reduced from one month to half a month; and the power of the Bank of Canada to vary the minimum cash ratio would be removed and replaced by a stand-by power, within certain limits and subject to certain notice requirements, to impose and vary a
Bank of Canada Act
minimum secondary reserve requirement, the secondary reserves to consist of cash reserves in excess of the statutory 7 per cent together with treasury bills and day-to-day loans. Should the Bank of Canada find it necessary to invoke the power to impose and vary the secondary reserve requirement, the bank could not set the initial requirement at more than 6 per cent of the chartered banks' Canadian dollar deposit liabilities and could not increase it by more than 1 per cent per month. In no case could the required ratio exceed 12 per cent. At the present time, by agreement with the Bank of Canada, the chartered banks maintain a secondary reserve of at least 7 per cent, in conjunction with an 8 per cent cash reserve.
The effect of these proposals would be to strengthen the instruments of monetary policy available to the Bank of Canada without adversely affecting the position of the chartered banks as compared with that of other financial institutions.
The proposed stand-by power would provide a means of impounding or releasing chartered bank liquidity-and thus influencing bank lending policies-which was supplementary to the more usual technique of changing the amount of cash reserves available to the banks in relation to the required level. The raising or lowering of secondary reserve requirements can exert this influence with less impact on interest rates and hence on international capital flows-a consideration which could be important in some circumstances. Such a stand-by power is not an unusual one for a central bank. In the United Kingdom the Bank of England has the power to call up special deposits, which is equivalent to raising secondary reserve requirements, and in the United States the Federal Reserve Board has the power to vary cash reserve requirements of commercial banks.
It is proposed to eliminate several sections which have been in the Act since 1934 but which have long been inoperative and which the Royal Commission recommended for removal. One of these covers the power of the Bank of Canada to act as banker or fiscal agent of the government of a province; this power has never been used and it would be difficult to exercise in a manner consistent with the bank's statutory responsibility in the field of monetary policy and as fiscal agent of the Government of Canada. Another section which it is proposed to remove is that which requires the bank to maintain a reserve

May 13. 1965
Bank of Canada Act
of gold and foreign exchange against its note and deposit liabilities and to redeem its notes in gold on demand; it ceased to have any practical meaning after the bank's holdings of gold and its holdings of foreign exchange, other than working balances, were transferred to the Government's Exchange Fund in 1940. A related amendment is proposed in respect of notes of the Bank of Canada to remove the description "payable to bearer on demand". Since these notes are themselves legal tender and have never, in fact, been convertible into gold, the present wording is unnecessary and in some quarters liable to misinterpretation.

Perhaps I should have put that into the singular and said "in one quarter".
The bill contains several provisions which affect the existing arrangements regarding directors and management of the Bank of Canada. Partners, officers or employees of firms of investment dealers which act as primary distributors of Government of Canada securities would be added to the list of those ineligible for appointment to the Bank's Board of Directors, on the ground that their business activities involve direct dealings with the central bank. The membership of the bank's executive committee would be enlarged by the appointment of an additional director, and the aggregate annual amount of directors' fees would be raised in order to permit more frequent meetings of the full board. It is also proposed that certain pension provisions relating to the Governor and Deputy Governor be made subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, as their appointment and salary now are. These features of the bill are in accord with the recommendations of the Royal Commission.
The remaining provisions of the bill involve a number of relatively minor technical matters which I do not propose to go into at this time. Hon. Members will, of course, have the opportunity of considering them in detail in committee along with the other matters dealt with in the bill.

speechtext:
In the circumstances I think I should reserve my comments both as to the principles and as to the details until there

has been an opportunity to study the content of the hon. gentleman's speech.
The bill itself, as the Minister has told us, touches upon a goodly number of minor matters. I should like to consider with care the implications of a gradual reduction from 8 per cent to 7 per cent of the cash reserve requirements before commenting further.
I am glad to learn that the Government intends to refer this bill to the Committee on Banking and Commerce. But before this can be done there is, of course, one thing which must happen. The Government must move expeditiously to have this committee set up, and at the moment there is no inkling of when this will be done. Perhaps the Minister would consult with the leader of the House and tell us just when that committee will be established. Have we to wait for the discussion of the proposals which the Government has put forward for amending the rules, and the possible adoption of those proposals either as they now stand or in an amended form? As a matter of fact, I think it might be better if the Government went right ahead and set up the Banking and Commerce Committee and let us get on with this type of work and with the Bank Act, because otherwise I think the Minister is going to find himself waiting for some time, because there may be some complications with regard to some of the changes in procedure which may not meet the acceptance of all sectors of the House. Therefore I would strongly recommend to the Minister that he have a talk with his colleague, the Government House Leader, in order to have this Committee set up and let us get on with it.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I am not going to rehash some of the difficulties that arose some years ago in the relationship with the then Governor of the Bank of Canada and the government of the day. All I can say is that I participated somewhat extensively in the debate and retract nothing I said at that time. I think, for the good of all, the air has been cleared, and this is the result of a course of conduct on the part of the Governor of the day that is quite unacceptable.
There is provision that the directors' fees may be doubled, and of course we know there are some changes with regard to the executive committee. I am not going to say anything about the implications of the consultation, the directive and the publication of a report, because I think the position of a Governor who has to receive orders in writing is already difficult. I think the Governor of
May 13. 1965

the bank is in the same position, shall we say, as a Deputy Minister with his Minister, and if it comes to pass in the relationship between the Minister and his Deputy Minister that the Deputy Minister has to insist to the Minister that a directive be put in writing, then the relationship is not as good as it should be.
I think that when the day comes that the Governor of the bank shall have to receive a written directive from the Minister on behalf of the Government, it will be rather a sorry one, and I do not know just how that position could be tolerated. In any event, it will make for a very interesting examination when that directive is tabled in Parliament and we get into the background as to why a written directive had to be issued.
I think, Mr. Speaker, I will limit my remarks to that point on this occasion. We will undoubtedly have a chance to discuss this question further. My colleague, the hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), will be back by the time we get into a further discussion of this bill, and undoubtedly he will have some comments to make.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I have about two or three minutes and I am not going to attempt to deal very exhaustively with this subject, beyond expressing my satisfaction that we have a Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) now who is prepared to forgo the luxury that I noted three of his predecessors seized upon, which was the luxury of hiding behind the actual, written text of the Bank of Canada Act and pretending that they had no control over or responsibility for monetary policy. The position is now clear, and we know where we have to fire the bullets if ever the occasion arises. I am very glad to see this. It was always rather frustrating before, when one wished to criticize our monetary policy, to have the Minister of Finance say, well, perhaps he agreed with it, but after all, he had nothing whatsoever to do with it because it was entirely up to the Governor of the Bank of Canada.
I think, as the hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has pointed out, if the occasion ever arose where these powers had to be exercised, the situation would already be extremely bad and I think it is very, very unlikely that the Minister is going to have to issue directives to the Governor of the Bank of Canada. In fact, it may be an instance where we are finally sort of tidying
Business of the House
up and putting into definite words a situation that was resolved during the unhappy period to which the hon. Member for Edmonton West referred a little while ago. As I say, Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable satisfaction that I see the Minister is now prepared to take full responsibility in this regard.
There is one other point with which I should like to deal at the present time. This is, that I notice we are also getting rid of another myth and and are finally pushing gold out of the picture, I presume on the understanding that the Canadian people are now sufficiently sophisticated to realize that in a modern currency gold plays no rational part. This brings me to another point, and I hope the Minister is listening. I hope he will not block, before the Banking and Commerce Committee, any attempt to have discussed what is, I think, another very serious thing with which we will simply have to deal before long. This is the whole question of international liquidity, which I think ties in with the fact that we have now heaved gold finally out of the picture with regard to the domestic situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext: Are you complaining?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, I am not complaining at all; I think it is a very sound idea. I think we are facing a very similar situation, or will be
before very long, in the international field, and I would hope that at the hearings of the Banking and Commerce Committee there might be an opportunity for that Committee to hear various experts on international monetary problems dealing with this question of the new developments which must take place within that area. It seems to me this is a place in which Canada could play a very important role.
I can understand the Minister's, perhaps, reluctance to provide a forum. I do not know whether he might feel it would cramp his style. I hope he will not, but will instead feel this will arm him in dealing with his fellow Ministers of Finance in the rest of the world and pressing for developments in the international field to bring the international monetary system into line with the modern managed monetary system that we have in the advanced countries.
May I call it ten o'clock, sir?
